source_read: PMC HTML full text PMC3844112 (accepted author manuscript; title confirmed): Abstract, all body sections, Table 1, Highlights, Acknowledgments and the Appendix of 62 study summaries read in full; the page text was cut off inside the reference list only. Figure 1 (nomological network diagram) not viewed.

claims.overstatement: No overstatement; the claim understates the source in one respect. It presents the cross-sectional evidence only as 'negative correlations in three studies in one paper by the author's team' (Kite, Pearson & Henson, 2013), whereas the review states that nearly every included study found that students reporting more strategies also reported drinking less and/or fewer problems (Introduction › Protective Behavioral Strategies, 2nd paragraph; Highlights), and the author ends by calling PBS use a promising way to reduce drinking and its consequences (Conclusion). The 'insufficient' judgment on whether more strategies lower drinking is consistent with the review's own 'mixed evidence' for prospective and mediation findings, but the claim should say that the same-sitting association is reported as near-universal and that the author's reading is more favourable. Small precision points: in Luebbe et al. (2009) strategy use was unrelated to both drinking and problems at the same time point (baseline and 4 months), not only to drinking; in Larimer et al. (2007) the intervention effect was described as fully, not partly, mediated; in Martens et al. (2011) prospective correlations with drinking were similar to the cross-sectional ones (only those with problems were weaker); one of the two day-by-day studies (Lewis et al., 2012) used 7-day recall at one sitting.
claims.note: Numbers checked: 62 studies; searches ended early February 2013; at least 11 measures; 80% (Abstract only, not derived in the body); 3 moderation studies (Benton 2004, Benton 2006, Borden 2011); 3 of 9 prospective correlations non-significant; 15-day diary, n = 40; 3 mediating trials and 3 trials without change in strategy use; 1 instruction experiment. Editors' count from the Appendix recomputed: studies with a trial, experiment, follow-up or daily design are 14 definite (nos. 2, 7, 12, 19, 23, 27, 31, 35, 36, 37, 47, 52, 55, 56) plus 2 ambiguous (26, 7-day recall; 38, pre- and post-matriculation in a sample the Appendix calls cross-sectional), so 46 to 48 of 62 otherwise, 74.2% to 77.4%: same as the claim's 74% to 77%. No advice on amounts or timing; strategies appear as studied behaviours.

anchors.extracted: Single author; APA PsycNet, Web of Science and Google Scholar searched with PBS and drinking-control-strategy terms, plus reference lists and forward citations of measure-development papers; college samples only; qualitative studies excluded; searches ended at the beginning of February 2013; 62 published studies, some with several samples and some samples in several reports, so the number of independent samples is unknown. No pooling.

anchors.locator: Introduction › Protective Behavioral Strategies, 1st paragraph; Measurement of PBS › Measurement summary
anchors.extracted: PBS examples: setting drinking limits, alternating alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks, avoiding drinking games, using a designated driver, not leaving a drink unattended, having a friend say when you have had enough; the common (narrow) definition is behaviours used immediately before, during and/or after drinking.

anchors.locator: Introduction › Protective Behavioral Strategies, 2nd paragraph; Highlights
anchors.extracted: Nearly every reviewed study supports that people who report more PBS also report drinking less and/or fewer alcohol-related problems (negative correlations with frequency, quantity, heavy episodes, estimated BAC and problem measures, examples cited); Highlights say PBS are consistently negatively correlated with problems. No effect sizes given.

anchors.locator: Measurement of PBS, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1, Time Window column
anchors.extracted: At least 11 PBS measures (PBSS, NCHA, CAS, PSQ, PBSM, SQ, SCQ and four unnamed), many in several variants; response scales contingent frequency (how often when drinking), absolute frequency (number of times), degree of truth or yes/no; absolute frequency conflates drinking frequency with strategy frequency. Table 1 shows no time window for most measures.

anchors.locator: Measurement of PBS › Variants of the PBSS, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: PBSS used in 36 studies (about 58%) in at least nine variants; no time window stated in 24 studies, 3 months in 5, a single day or occasion in 4.

anchors.locator: Measurement of PBS › SQ, 1st paragraph; Appendix no. 18
anchors.extracted: SQ Strategies Used While Drinking correlated positively with alcohol outcomes on the original absolute-frequency scale; three studies that changed the response scale (Kite, Pearson & Henson, 2013) found the positive link is due to that scale, and with a contingent-frequency scale correlations with alcohol outcomes were consistently negative.

anchors.locator: Moderators of the Relationships between PBS Use and Alcohol-Related Outcomes › Alcohol use, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Higher reported PBS use weakened the positive alcohol use-problems association in Benton et al. (2004), Benton et al. (2006; two modest samples) and Borden et al. (2011); the first and last had very large samples. No effect sizes.

anchors.locator: Review of Evidence for PBS as a Mechanism of Change › Randomized controlled trials, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Three RCTs with significant mediation by PBS: Larimer et al. (2007), mailed personalized feedback, effect on alcohol involvement at 12 months fully mediated by PBS change baseline to 12 months; Barnett et al. (2007), brief motivational interview in mandated students, PBS at 3 months mediated drinks per day at 12 months; Murphy et al. (2012), small trial, PBS change to 1 month mediated problems at 6 months. Three RCTs (Kulesza 2010, Neighbors 2009, Walters 2009) did not change PBS. The author treats the mediations as among the strongest causal evidence.

anchors.locator: Review of Evidence for PBS as a Mechanism of Change › Other experimental designs, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Sugarman & Carey (2009): students instructed to increase PBS reported more PBS but did not reduce drinking; PBS change scores not correlated with alcohol change scores. Walters et al. (2009): repeated assessment raised reported PBS and lowered reported drinking against delayed assessment (assessment reactivity).

anchors.locator: Review of Evidence for PBS as a Mechanism of Change › Non-experimental longitudinal designs, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Martens, Cimini et al. (2007), single group: PBS rose at 6 weeks after a brief intervention, change not correlated with alcohol outcomes. Martens et al. (2011): prospective correlations with drinking similar to cross-sectional ones, with problems weaker (3 of 9 non-significant). Luebbe et al. (2009), women: PBS did not predict drinking or problems concurrently at baseline or 4 months, but baseline PBS predicted fewer problems at 4 months adjusting for baseline problems, drinking and risk behaviours. Author: mixed evidence.

anchors.locator: Review of Evidence for PBS as a Mechanism of Change › Designs with daily PBS reports, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Two multilevel studies: Lewis et al. (2012), 7-day retrospective daily reports around the 21st birthday; Pearson, D'Lima & Kelley (2013), 15-day daily diary. Daily Manner of Drinking strategies went with less drinking; daily Limiting/Stopping strategies with more drinking (and problems or positive consequences); Serious Harm Reduction strategies with more drinking between and within persons and more problems on the days used. Author's explanation: some strategies, such as a designated driver, may be planned when heavy drinking is intended.

anchors.locator: Identifying Gaps in Knowledge › Ecological bias and Recall bias, 1st paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Vast majority of studies cross-sectional and between-person, so within-person inference is an ecological fallacy; nearly every study measured PBS and outcomes only by retrospective self-report, often with no time window; only three studies reduced recall bias (Frank 2012 and Neighbors 2009, one occasion; Pearson 2013, daily diary, n = 40).

anchors.locator: Identifying Gaps in Knowledge › Weak tests of PBS use as a mechanism of change, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: None of the mediating interventions primarily targeted PBS; temporal-relation evidence weak; no dose-response shown; other mechanisms not assessed (specificity).

Of the 62 reports, 80% reported only cross-sectional data (no derivation in the body or Appendix; editors' recount 74% to 77%); only two attempted to reduce recall bias (the body names three); two examined both within- and between-person effects.

Intervention, experimental and longitudinal research give mixed evidence for PBS as a mediator and as a prospective predictor; a meta-analysis is needed; the final sentence nonetheless calls PBS use a promising way to reduce drinking and its consequences.

key_findings.correction: Refinement: the body says Larimer et al.'s effect was fully mediated.

Refinement: in Luebbe et al. (2009) PBS were unrelated to both drinking and problems at the same time point (baseline and 4 months); in Martens et al. (2011) prospective correlations with drinking were similar to the cross-sectional ones.

reporting_issues.note: Recount gives 14 definite plus 2 ambiguous non-cross-sectional studies (Appendix nos. 26 and 38), 74.2% to 77.4%.
Table 1 PBSS rows recounted: 33 listings (16 five-point, 13 six-point, 4 yes/no; time windows 24 none, 5 three-month, 4 single day or occasion).
Checked in the page DOM: no bold or underline elements in Table 1; the only underlined items are the 65 citation links.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall some concerns, agreed. Seven of the 62 included studies have the author as co-author, as the card says.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the abstract and most of the body are cautious; the overreach is in the Highlights ('consistently' negative) and the final sentence, as the card states.

missed: No key finding records the review's own summary of the cross-sectional evidence: nearly every included study found that students reporting more PBS reported drinking less and/or fewer problems (Introduction › Protective Behavioral Strategies, 2nd paragraph). It sits only in the interpretation gap, and the claim omits it.

Change-score findings that favour PBS are not recorded: in a non-efficacious peer intervention, change in each PBS subscale correlated negatively with change in one to three alcohol outcomes (Cimini et al., 2009; Appendix no. 7), and in its panel follow-up Manner of Drinking change predicted fewer drinks per week at 6 and 12 months (Martens et al., 2011; Non-experimental longitudinal designs paragraph).
